discipline_framing: Cultural evolution, internet meme studies, and diffusion science applied to the replication, mutation, and selection of viral ideas
audience: Trend analysts, cultural strategists, social media researchers, and brand teams who must explain and anticipate how memes and viral content evolve and spread
sources: Dawkins, The Selfish Gene (the meme concept) and the subsequent memetics literature (Dennett, Blackmore, Journal of Memetics archive)
Shifman, Memes in Digital Culture (MIT Press) — internet meme studies, participatory culture, memetic dimensions
Berger, Contagious (STEPPS framework) and Berger & Milkman's empirical study of most-emailed content
Know Your Meme and meme-documentation practice as primary genealogical sources
Cheng, Adamic, Kleinberg lineage on cascade prediction and viral dynamics research
Miltner & Highfield, Wiggins, Milner, and Phillips (This Is Why We Can't Have Nice Things) on meme communities, politics, and ambivalence
Coleman and folklore/digital-culture scholarship on memes as folk expression
pitfalls: Treating memetics' gene analogy literally — memes lack clear units, fidelity, and copying mechanisms, and the critiques matter for analysis
Confusing virality (a spread pattern) with quality, truth, or representativeness of an audience
Attributing spread to content features alone while ignoring platform amplification, timing, and network position
Assuming meme adoption signals endorsement — irony, ambivalence, and participation without belief are the norm
Trend-jacking memes without understanding community ownership and context, triggering backlash
